title: Why the Author's Intent Is the Meaning
subtitle: A defense of authorial intent in biblical interpretation, why the meaning of a text is what the author meant and not what the reader makes of it, and how this single conviction protects the Bible from becoming a mirror

sections.title: What Does It Mean to You
sections.body:
We have all sat in the Bible study where the leader reads a verse and asks the fatal question. What does this verse mean to you. And around the circle it goes, each person offering a private impression, none of them asking what the verse actually says.

It is a kind word, and a disastrous one. Because a text does not have a different meaning for every reader. It has the meaning its author put there.

When you ask what a text means to you, you have quietly made yourself the source of the meaning. You have turned the Bible from a word God spoke into a mirror that reflects whatever you bring to it. This is the most polite heresy in the modern church, and it is everywhere. The conviction that fights it is simple and old. The meaning of a text is what the author meant by it. Not what it makes you feel. Not what you can make it say. What he meant. Lose that, and you have lost the ability to be addressed by anyone but yourself.

sections.title: Communication Itself Requires It
sections.body:
This is not first a rule about the Bible. It is how all human communication works. When you read a letter from your wife, you are not trying to discover what the words mean to you. You are trying to discover what she meant. To do otherwise would not be reading. It would be using her words as an excuse to talk to yourself.

A text is an act of communication by a person who intended to say something. To read is to recover what they intended.

The whole point of language is that one mind can reach another. I write these words meaning something definite, and you do me the basic courtesy of trying to find out what. The moment you decide the words mean whatever you want, communication has stopped, and what remains is only your own reflection wearing my vocabulary. This is true of a road sign, a contract, a love letter, and the Word of God. Meaning is anchored in the will of the one who spoke. Cut that anchor and meaning floats away entirely, and every reading becomes as good and as worthless as every other.

sections.title: When the Reader Becomes the Maker
sections.body:
The opposing view has a respectable academic pedigree, but stripped of its dress it says this. The reader makes the meaning. The text is raw material, and what counts is the reading, the response, the way the words land in your particular life. The author is dead, the saying goes, and the reader is free.

Follow that road to its end and the Bible cannot rebuke you, cannot surprise you, cannot tell you anything you did not already think.

A text that means whatever the reader makes it mean can never correct the reader. It can only confirm him. The slaveholder found his slavery in it, the comfortable found their comfort, and there was no fixed meaning standing outside them to say no, that is not what this says. When meaning lives in the reader, Scripture loses its power to stand over us and judge us, which is the very thing it was given to do. A Bible that only echoes you is not authority. It is a captive. The reader who makes the meaning has not freed the text. He has silenced it and kept only his own voice.

sections.title: Two Authors, One Meaning
sections.body:
Someone will object that Scripture has a divine author as well as a human one, and that God may have meant more than the prophet knew. That is true, and it does not overturn the rule. It deepens it.

The divine intent never contradicts the human author's words. It fills them fuller along the same line, the way the New Testament finds Christ in texts the prophets only dimly grasped.

Isaiah meant something real and definite when he wrote, and the Spirit who carried him meant that and more, as the whole canon would later reveal. But the fuller meaning grows out of the words the human author actually wrote, in the direction they actually pointed. It is not a secret meaning unhooked from the text, available only to the spiritually clever. It is the same meaning, seen at last in the light of Christ, to whom the human author was always being led. So we still ask what the author meant. We simply read his intent within the larger intent of the divine Author who inspired him, never against the grain of his words.

sections.title: The Discipline This Demands
sections.body:
Authorial intent is not a power you seize. It is a humility you submit to. It means coming to the text ready to be told something you did not already believe, by someone who is not you, who lived long ago, in a world you must work to enter.

It is harder than the alternative. It is easier to ask what a verse means to me than to do the labor of finding out what the author meant.

That labor is real. You study the words, the context, the situation the author wrote into, the argument he was making. You read the men and women who have done this work before you. You hold your first impressions loosely and let the text correct them. This is slower and less flattering than free association, and it is the only way to actually hear God rather than yourself. The reward is worth the cost. A text whose meaning you cannot control is a text that can finally save you, because it can finally tell you the truth instead of agreeing with you.

sections.title: Let the Author Speak
sections.body:
So put away the question of what a verse means to you, and take up the harder and better one. What did the author mean. Submit to that, and the Bible can address you. Refuse it, and you will only ever hear your own voice reading aloud.

The meaning is not yours to make. It is the author's to give, and yours to receive.

I have caught myself reading my own preferences into a passage and calling it the Spirit's leading, and the correction was always the same. Go back. Ask what he meant. The discipline of authorial intent is finally an act of reverence. It treats the words of God as words that say something whether I like it or not. That is the only kind of Bible worth having. A mirror cannot save you. A word from outside you can. Let the author speak, and stop putting your words in his mouth.
